# NitroIDE — full context for LLMs

> Version: 2026-11-10 (v30.5). This file is updated on every release.
> NitroIDE is a free, open-source, client-side browser IDE. Write HTML, CSS, and JavaScript with the Monaco editor, see live preview with hot module replacement, inject CDN libraries, and export your project as a ZIP — no account, no installation — your code runs only in your browser.

## Scope (important)
- Frontend-only: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. No Node.js, no backend, no database.
- NitroIDE cannot run server-side code, host APIs, or replace CodeSandbox/Replit-style backends.
- What it is for: instant frontend coding, prototyping, learning, demos, and shareable snippets.

## Pricing
- 100% free, no account required, no paywall. Free forever — the only plan.
- The AI pair programmer uses your own provider API keys — Groq, Gemini, and OpenRouter offer free tiers; NitroIDE charges nothing for AI. See https://nitroide.com/pricing.md

## What's new in v30.5 (October 2026)
- Listed on 9 software directories (DevHunt, AlternativeTo, SaaSHub, SourceForge, directree, IndieTools, Fazier, NoLogin, TinyShelf) with a redesigned homepage badge row.
- Daily publishing across X, LinkedIn, Peerlist, Hashnode and Coder Legion, mirrored on the Ecosystem Pulse page; blog library now 46 articles.
- Trust and support: Trustpilot profile with public reviews, Ko-fi donations live, GitHub Sponsors approved.
- Whole-site light-mode readability: light values for brand and code colors, fixed contact inputs, palette, footer, modal and stop-button contrast, dark variants for all article accent colors.
- Deep audit pass (68 files): sitemap trimmed to 91 URLs in the Oct 31 audit pass; now 97 URLs, RSS fixed, icon fonts cut from 403KB to 19KB, service worker and forms hardened.
- Directory badges fixed after a browser-isolation header blocked cross-origin images (header now credentialless, WebContainer WASM unaffected).
- Templates "Open in NitroIDE" buttons readable in both themes.

## AI pair programmer (new in v30, October 2026)
- Built-in AI pair programmer: a conversational chat in a right-hand sidebar inside the IDE workspace.
- Bring your own key (BYOK): works with Groq, Gemini, OpenRouter, OpenAI, and SambaNova (via a non-storing proxy). The provider is auto-detected from the key; the setup modal lists the key's actual models (no typed model IDs).
- Privacy: for Groq, Gemini, OpenRouter, and OpenAI, the browser talks directly to the chosen AI provider. SambaNova passes through a non-storing Cloudflare Worker proxy. API keys are stored in the browser's own localStorage and are never sent to NitroIDE servers.
- Smart file selection: the AI sees the attached files (index.html, style.css, script.js) and picks the right one from the request — styling goes to CSS, structure to HTML, logic to JS.
- Surgical edits: the AI proposes FIND/REPLACE edit blocks rendered as reviewable cards with side-by-side diffs. Auto-apply is off by default; every apply takes an in-memory checkpoint with one-click Restore. Ambiguous or unknown edit targets are refused rather than guessed.
- Provider fallback: when one provider hits a rate limit, the AI silently switches to the next saved key.

## Privacy
- Your code runs only in your browser and is never sent to NitroIDE servers.
- Analytics is Google Analytics 4 only (loads for every visitor; page addresses are sanitized to path + utm_* params); no other telemetry.
- Contact/feedback forms go to a Cloudflare Worker that emails the operator via Resend. Newsletter uses Buttondown. Share links compress the workspace into the URL itself (?code=) — nothing is uploaded.
- See the privacy policy: https://nitroide.com/legal.html#privacy

## Offline
- Works offline after first load (PWA + service worker).

## Sharing and embedding
- Sharing: the Share button generates a `?code=` link containing the compressed workspace.
- Embedding: append `?embed=1` to the workspace URL for a chromeless embed.
- Import: `?gist=<id>` loads a GitHub Gist, `?url=<raw-file-url>` imports a raw file, `?template=<slug>` loads a starter template.
- API: `Nitro.watch(name, data)` renders a live, syntax-highlighted JSON tree of any watched value in the IDE's State tab. See https://nitroide.com/docs.html

## Full article text

### The Codebox Engine: How Editor, Preview and Console Stay in Sync Without a Server
Source: https://nitroide.com/blog/codebox-engine.html
Date: November 2026

Every browser IDE has the same three panes: the editor on one side, the live preview on the other, and a console somewhere underneath. What users never see is the plumbing between them — and in a tool with no server, that plumbing has to do all the work a backend normally would.

NitroIDE's codebox is three Monaco editor instances, one sandboxed iframe, and a console panel, all coordinated by a small engine that lives entirely in your browser. Here is how it actually works.

## Three editors, one workspace

The workspace is three files — index.html, style.css and script.js — and each one gets its own Monaco instance. Monaco is the editor engine behind VS Code, so the typing experience is the real thing: syntax highlighting, bracket matching, Emmet, find and replace. But the interesting part is not the editing. It is that the three editors are treated as one source of truth: the engine reads their current contents whenever it needs to rebuild, and nothing about your code ever leaves the machine to do it.

## The preview is a document, not a page

The live preview is an <iframe> whose srcdoc attribute is rebuilt from your three files every time you type. There is no server rendering anything, no dev server, no hot-module-replacement protocol. The parent page assembles a complete HTML document in memory — your HTML, your CSS injected, your JavaScript injected — and hands it to the iframe as a string. The browser renders it.

That is why the preview feels instant, and also why it can feel wrong. Rebuilding a whole document on every keystroke would flicker and churn, so the engine debounces: HTML and JavaScript edits wait 500 ms after you stop typing before a rebuild is triggered. CSS edits are cheaper and faster. The debounce is the difference between a live preview and a strobe light.

The iframe runs sandboxed — allow-scripts allow-modals allow-popups allow-forms — which is the part that keeps the whole arrangement safe. Your preview code can run, show alerts, open popups and submit forms, but it cannot reach the parent page, touch your saved projects, or read anything outside its own little document. A shared link that opens someone else's code renders in the same sandbox, which is exactly why opening a stranger's link is safe: the code runs, and it runs nowhere near your stuff.

## Talking across the wall

The editor and the preview are in different worlds — the parent page and the sandboxed iframe — so they communicate the only way the web allows across that boundary: postMessage. The engine uses it in both directions. The parent pushes new code in; the preview pushes console output and errors back out.

That return channel is what makes the console panel work. When your preview code calls console.log, the message does not vanish into the iframe's devtools. It is forwarded to the parent and rendered in NitroIDE's own console tab, with error badges when something throws. And the console input line at the bottom works the other way: type JavaScript there and it executes against the running preview, so you can poke at your page's state live — inspect a variable, call a function, change a value — without touching the editor.

This is the piece I am proudest of, because it closes the loop. Editor, preview and console are not three features sharing a screen; they are one feedback loop. Type, see it render, read what it printed, poke it from the console, type again. The loop is the product.

## The flicker, and why swaps wait for paint

For a while, the loop had a visible flaw: the preview flickered — a black flash, sometimes white — on every rebuild. The first fix stacked the incoming iframe behind the live one and lengthened the debounce, and it did not work. The flicker survived, which meant the problem was not the timing of the rebuild. It was the timing of the swap.

The fix that landed was to stop swapping on a timer and start swapping on evidence: the new preview only replaces the old one after it has actually painted, with a 1.5-second fallback so a slow page never hangs the editor. Waiting for paint instead of waiting for a clock is a small change with a general lesson in it — when a UI glitch survives a timing fix, the timing was probably never the problem. The thing you are waiting for is.

## Why no server is a feature here, not a limitation

A server-backed IDE syncs editor, preview and console through a backend: your keystrokes travel up, a build runs somewhere, results travel down. That architecture buys collaboration and persistence, and it costs latency on every keystroke and a dependency on a connection.

The codebox engine buys the opposite. Everything happens in one browser process, so the loop is as fast as the machine you are sitting at — there is no network round-trip between typing and seeing. It works offline, because there is nothing to be online for. And it is private by construction: the code never leaves your machine, because there is nowhere for it to go.

The trade-off is honest and worth naming. No server means no live collaboration and no cloud sync — your projects live in your browser's storage, and moving them means exporting them. That is the deal the whole tool makes, and the codebox is where you feel it most directly: the speed and the privacy are the same architectural choice.

Three panes, one engine, zero servers. Type, see, read, poke, repeat — that loop is the whole IDE.

## Frequently asked questions

### Why does the preview run in a sandboxed iframe?

The sandbox is what keeps preview code away from the rest of the tool. Preview code can run, show alerts and submit forms, but it cannot reach the parent page, touch saved projects, or read anything outside its own document — which is why opening a stranger's shared link is safe.

### How does NitroIDE's console capture output from the preview?

The parent page and the sandboxed iframe talk over postMessage in both directions. The preview forwards console.log calls and errors to the parent, which renders them in NitroIDE's console tab. The console input line works the other way: JavaScript typed there executes against the running preview.

### Why did the preview flicker on every rebuild?

The swap was happening on a timer, before the new frame had actually painted. The fix swaps only after the new preview has painted, with a 1.5-second fallback so a slow page never hangs the editor. When a UI glitch survives a timing fix, the timing was probably never the problem.

### Privacy as a Feature: Your Code Never Leaves Your Machine
Source: https://nitroide.com/blog/privacy-as-a-feature.html
Date: November 2026

Your code is the most personal thing you type all day. It holds half-formed ideas, client work, passwords you meant to move, and the project you have not told anyone about yet. Most online editors treat that as cargo: the moment you type, it travels to a server, gets stored in someone else's database, and is governed by someone else's retention policy and breach history.

NitroIDE takes a different position, and it is not a policy page. It is the architecture. There is no server to send your code to.

## The architecture that makes the claim true

NitroIDE has no server and no database. That sentence does most of the work in this article, so it is worth being precise about what it means.

Your projects live in your browser, in localStorage — the same machine you typed them on, under the same origin as the editor. Close the tab, restart the browser, come back on Monday: the work is still there, because it never left. There is no account to create, no sync queue to fail, and no backend that could leak a database it does not have.

This is a tradeoff stated up front, not a footnote. Code that lives only in one browser lives only in that browser. There is no cross-device sync to fall back on, and clearing that browser's site data will take your projects with it. That is why ZIP export exists: the portable copy is yours to keep, in a file you control, rather than an account you rent. Local-first means you are the backup strategy, and the honest version of this article says so instead of pretending otherwise.

## What "never leaves your machine" actually means

The claim is deliberately narrow, and the narrowness is the point. It means your project files are never uploaded to a NitroIDE server, because there is no NitroIDE server side to upload them to. Your code is read and written by JavaScript running in your own browser tab.

It does not mean your code is sealed in a vault. Anything running in your browser tab can, in principle, see what that tab can see — which is why NitroIDE's own design keeps untrusted code out of the editor's origin (more on the preview sandbox below), and why the next section matters more than this one: the moment you choose to share, the rules change, and they change because you changed them.

## Sharing without a server

Sharing is where most "private" tools quietly become servers. The usual flow uploads your project, stores it, and hands back an ID. Anyone with the ID asks the server for your code.

NitroIDE's share engine skips the server entirely. The Share button compresses the whole workspace into a ?code= URL parameter, and opening that link rebuilds the workspace locally in the reader's browser. Nothing passes through NitroIDE on the way, because there is no middle to pass through. The link itself is the transport, and the reader's browser is the destination.

That design has a consequence worth saying out loud: a share link IS you handing your code to whoever receives it — via the URL, not via a server. Anyone with the link can open it and read the project. URLs get pasted into chats, forwarded, screenshotted, and logged by proxies. So the rule is simple and non-negotiable: never put secrets, tokens, or passwords in a project you plan to share, and never share a link you would not want forwarded. The privacy guarantee covers the tool not taking your code. It cannot cover you giving it away.

The same URL-carried design sets a size limit, too. A very large project makes a very long URL, and very long URLs break in chats and address bars. For a demo or a tutorial example — a handful of files, one concept — that never matters. For a full application, export a ZIP and share a small, focused demo of the idea instead. The share link is for the example, not the app.

## The preview sandbox: why shared code cannot touch your projects

The sharpest privacy question is not about NitroIDE's code. It is about other people's code. When you open a share link, you are running code someone else wrote. If that code could reach into your saved projects, the whole local-first story would collapse.

It cannot, by construction. NitroIDE's preview runs in a sandboxed iframe with an opaque origin, which is what keeps code in a shared link — or in a preview — from touching the reader's saved projects or the editor's localStorage. The preview cannot read your project list, rewrite your files, or exfiltrate your store, because from the browser's point of view it lives nowhere near them.

The tradeoff, stated in the embeds article and repeated here because it bites the same way: localStorage, sessionStorage, and cookies are unavailable inside the preview, and in Safari, touching them throws a SecurityError. Demo code that reads storage unguarded will crash inside the preview while working fine in a normal tab. Wrap storage access in try/catch in any code you plan to share, and the same demo runs everywhere. A sandbox that let shared code touch your storage would not be a sandbox.

There is a second edge to the same rule, on your side of the editor. localStorage has no per-key permissions: any script running on the editor's own origin could read the whole store. Never put tokens or secrets in a project at all — not because NitroIDE will leak them, but because a browser store is not a vault, and the safest secret is one that was never typed into the project in the first place.

## Why this is a feature, not a missing backend

It is tempting to read "no server" as an unfinished product — the backend that has not been built yet. I read it the other way around. Every backend is a liability surface: an account database to breach, a retention policy to get wrong, a subpoena target, a bill that eventually needs paying by someone, usually the user. Removing the backend removes that whole class of failure at once. There is no NitroIDE database of your code to leak, to sell, or to lose, because the database was never built.

That also changes the relationship between the tool and the person using it. A cloud IDE needs your account because its business model needs your data to live on its servers. A local-first IDE does not. No signup wall stands between you and the editor, and no "free tier" clock starts ticking on your projects, because your projects were never anyone else's asset.

The honest summary is this: your code stays on your machine until you decide otherwise — by sharing a link, or by exporting a file. Those are your decisions, made in the open, with the consequences visible. Everything else is architecture, not a promise. And architecture, unlike a promise, cannot quietly change its mind in a terms-of-service update.

## Frequently asked questions

### Where does NitroIDE store my projects?

In your browser's localStorage, on the same machine you typed them on. There is no server and no database, so nothing is uploaded anywhere.

### Can someone else's shared code read my saved projects?

No. The preview runs in a sandboxed iframe with an opaque origin, so code in a share link or preview cannot reach the editor's localStorage or your project list.

### What is the catch with local-first storage?

Your projects live in one browser: no cross-device sync, and clearing site data removes them. ZIP export is the portable backup. And a share link hands your code to whoever receives it, so never put secrets in a project you plan to share.

### Embeds: Putting a Live NitroIDE Playground Inside Your Docs
Source: https://nitroide.com/blog/embeds-live-playground-in-docs.html
Date: October 2026

Every tutorial has the same weak spot: the code sample. A static block shows what the code looks like. It cannot show what the code does. The reader has to copy it, open an editor, paste it, and run it — and every step in that chain is a step where a reader leaves.

A month ago I wrote about NitroIDE's share engine: the Share button compresses an entire workspace into a ?code= URL parameter, and opening that link rebuilds the workspace locally in the reader's browser. Nothing is uploaded to a server. That post was about sending code to one person. This one is about the layer on top of it: embedding that workspace inside a page, so the reader never has to leave the tutorial at all.

## One parameter turns a share link into an embed

Take any NitroIDE share URL and add ?embed=1 to it. That is the whole API:

<iframe src="https://nitroide.com/tools/codebox.html?embed=1&code=YOUR_SHARE_CODE" width="100%" height="500" frameborder="0"></iframe>
 The embed loads a stripped-down, read-only viewer. The full IDE chrome is gone — no file explorer, no console panel, no settings menus. What remains is the two things a reader actually needs: the editor and the live preview, side by side. The reader sees the code and its output in the same frame, on the same page, with nothing to install and no account to create.

Read-only is a deliberate choice, not a missing feature. A tutorial embed is not a workspace; it is a demonstration. If the reader could edit the code in place, every edit would be a fork of the author's example with no way back — and the next reader would see someone else's experiment, not the tutorial. So the embed shows, and the escape hatch handles editing: every embed carries a footer link reading "Built with NitroIDE — open & edit". One click opens the exact workspace in the full editor, where the reader can change anything. Show first, edit second, and never confuse the two.

## Where this actually belongs

The honest answer is: anywhere that renders an iframe and where the reader is there to learn. Blog posts, documentation pages, tutorial sites, course material — anywhere a code sample currently sits as a dead block.

It does not belong in a GitHub README. GitHub strips iframes from rendered Markdown, so an embed pasted into a README renders as nothing. That is what the "Open in NitroIDE" badge is for — a link, not a frame — and knowing which of the two a surface accepts is the difference between an embed that works and one that silently vanishes. If the page cannot render an iframe, do not force the embed in; link out instead.

The second place it belongs is less obvious: your own changelog and release notes. A new feature described in prose is a claim; the same feature embedded as a running demo is evidence. When a release note says "the preview now updates without flicker," an embedded playground running the new behaviour lets the reader verify it in ten seconds instead of trusting the sentence.

## The details that make an embed feel native, not bolted on

A bare iframe works. A few attributes make it feel like part of the page:

None of these are NitroIDE features. They are the hosting page's job, and they are the difference between an embed that feels like part of the tutorial and one that feels pasted in.

## The limits, stated plainly

An embed inherits every limit of the share link it is built on. The workspace travels inside the URL itself, compressed into the ?code= parameter, so a very large project makes a very long URL. For a tutorial demo — a handful of files, a single concept — that is never a problem. For a full application, it is: use ZIP export for the project and embed a small, focused demo of the idea instead. The embed is for the example, not the app.

The second limit comes from the preview's sandbox. NitroIDE's preview runs in a sandboxed iframe with an opaque origin, which is what keeps code in a shared link from touching the reader's saved projects. The tradeoff is that localStorage, sessionStorage, and cookies are unavailable inside the preview — and in Safari, touching them throws a SecurityError. Demo code that reads localStorage unguarded will crash inside the embed while working fine in a normal tab. Wrap storage access in try/catch in any code you plan to embed, and the same demo runs everywhere.

The third limit is the read-only viewer itself. It hides the console, so a demo whose point is console output — logging, errors, debugging — loses its punchline inside an embed. That is a real constraint, and the honest response is to pick the right surface: embed the demos whose output is visual, and link out to the full editor for the ones whose output lives in the console.

## Why this matters more than a nicer code block

Syntax highlighting made code readable. Embeds make it runnable, and that is a different category of change. A readable sample asks the reader to trust the author. A runnable sample lets the reader check the author — change a value, watch the preview move, break it, fix it. That is the feedback loop NitroIDE is built around, except now it happens inside someone else's docs, for a reader who never opened the IDE at all.

The embed is also the quietest distribution NitroIDE has. Every embed carries its own attribution in the footer, and every footer click is a reader who arrived at the full editor from inside a tutorial they were already reading — not from a post, not from an ad, from a working demo. That is the growth loop that does not look like a growth loop: make the tool useful inside other people's pages, and let the pages do the talking.

One parameter, one iframe, one running demo where a dead code block used to be. Try it with the docs example above — paste a share code into the snippet, drop it into a page, and the tutorial stops describing the code and starts running it.

## Try it

I build NitroIDE — a browser-based IDE where your code never leaves your machine: nitroide.com

⭐ If you enjoyed this, star NitroIDE on GitHub: github.com/nitroideofficial/nitroide

## Frequently asked questions

### How do you embed a NitroIDE playground in a page?

Take any NitroIDE share URL, add ?embed=1 to it, and drop it in an iframe. It loads a stripped-down, read-only viewer with just the editor and the live preview — no file explorer, console panel, or settings menus.

### Why is the embed read-only?

A tutorial embed is a demonstration, not a workspace. If readers could edit in place, the next reader would see someone else's experiment instead of the tutorial. The footer link "Built with NitroIDE — open & edit" opens the exact workspace in the full editor for anyone who wants to change it.

### Where should you not use a NitroIDE embed?

GitHub READMEs strip iframes from rendered Markdown, so an embed there renders as nothing — link out with the "Open in NitroIDE" badge instead. And demos whose point is console output lose their punchline, because the embed hides the console; those belong in the full editor.

### JSON-LD Recipes: BlogPosting, FAQPage, and SoftwareApplication Without a Plugin
Source: https://nitroide.com/blog/json-ld-recipes-no-plugin.html
Date: October 2026

Two weeks ago I wrote the overview: a static indie site needs three machine-readable files — sitemap, schema, and llms.txt. That post told you what each one is for. This one is the part I left out on purpose: the actual code.

I run NitroIDE, a browser IDE on a static host with no server, no build step, and no plugin system. There is no SEO plugin to install, so every block of structured data on the site is a <script type="application/ld+json"> block I wrote by hand. Three recipes cover almost everything an indie site needs. Copy them, change the values, validate before shipping — and, crucially, keep them honest, because schema that describes content the page does not show is a mismatch waiting to be flagged.

## Recipe 1: SoftwareApplication — the product page

This one lives on the homepage and answers a single question: what is this thing? For NitroIDE it names the product, its category, that it runs in a web browser, that it is free, and the features a human would actually recognise from the page. Here is the shape, trimmed to the fields that matter:

{
 "@context": "https://schema.org",
 "@type": "SoftwareApplication",
 "name": "NitroIDE",
 "applicationCategory": "DeveloperApplication",
 "operatingSystem": "Web Browser",
 "url": "https://nitroide.com/",
 "isAccessibleForFree": true,
 "description": "NitroIDE is a zero-latency, client-side browser IDE featuring the Monaco editor, live preview, offline support, and a built-in AI pair-programmer for HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.",
 "featureList": [
 "Client-side HTML, CSS, and JavaScript editing",
 "Instant live preview",
 "ZIP export",
 "Offline-ready browser workspace"
 ],
 "author": { "@type": "Person", "name": "Yash Panchal" }
}
 Three rules I follow for this one. First, operatingSystem for a web tool is "Web Browser" — not Windows, not macOS, not a list of platforms the tool never shipped on. Second, every item in featureList must be a feature the homepage actually shows; the moment the list becomes aspirational, the schema is lying in a format machines trust. Third, one block, one product. If you are tempted to add a second SoftwareApplication block for a different page, you probably need a different type for that page, not a duplicate.

The mistake that voids this recipe is version drift. NitroIDE's real block carries a softwareVersion field, and it changes in the same commit as the version it describes. A SoftwareApplication block that still claims last month's version is not a small inaccuracy — it is the product's identity, wrong, in the one place a machine reads it.

## Recipe 2: BlogPosting — every article

Every blog article on NitroIDE carries a compact BlogPosting block in its <head>. It is deliberately small: headline, description, author, publisher, the page URL, and two dates. Small is a feature. A BlogPosting block with twenty fields, half of them guessed, is worse than this one, because every guessed field is a future mismatch.

{
 "@context": "https://schema.org",
 "@type": "BlogPosting",
 "headline": "How NitroIDE Renders Code Instantly: srcdoc + postMessage",
 "description": "NitroIDE's preview renders with near-zero latency: one sandboxed iframe, srcdoc rendering, an anti-flicker swap, and postMessage updates. Honest tradeoffs.",
 "author": { "@type": "Person", "name": "Yash Panchal", "url": "https://nitroide.com/about.html#author" },
 "publisher": { "@type": "Organization", "name": "NitroIDE" },
 "mainEntityOfPage": "https://nitroide.com/blog/0ms-preview-srcdoc-postmessage-no-bundler.html",
 "datePublished": "2026-09-26",
 "dateModified": "2026-09-26"
}
 Two fields do more work than they look like they should. mainEntityOfPage is the canonical URL of the article itself — it is what ties this block to this page and stops a copied block from describing the wrong URL. And dateModified is the field that makes updates visible: when I correct or extend an article, dateModified moves and datePublished does not. An article that was fixed last week but whose schema still says it is untouched is telling machines it is older than it is.

The mistake that voids this recipe is copy-paste without editing. It is the easiest block to clone across articles, which makes it the easiest to ship with the previous article's headline, description, or URL still in it. Every new article gets a fresh block, and the check is one line: does mainEntityOfPage equal the URL of the page I am looking at?

## Recipe 3: FAQPage — only where the page really answers questions

FAQPage is the most abused of the three, so it gets the strictest rule: only use it where the page visibly contains those questions and answers. NitroIDE articles end with a real FAQ section, and the schema mirrors it exactly — same questions, same answers, in the same words. Here is one pair from the preview-architecture article:

{
 "@context": "https://schema.org",
 "@type": "FAQPage",
 "mainEntity": [
 {
 "@type": "Question",
 "name": "How does the preview update so fast?",
 "acceptedAnswer": {
 "@type": "Answer",
 "text": "One sandboxed srcdoc iframe, incremental postMessage updates with CSS patched in place, and an anti-flicker double-buffer swap — no bundler, no server round-trip."
 }
 }
 ]
}
 Note what is not in the answer: no marketing, no link, no call to action. An accepted answer is an answer, and the moment it becomes a pitch, the whole block reads as markup written for the search result rather than for the reader. That is exactly the pattern that gets FAQ rich results withdrawn.

The mistake that voids this recipe is the mirror breaking. The FAQ section on the page changes — a question gets reworded, an answer gets corrected — and the schema does not. Now the page and its schema disagree, in public, in a format designed to be machine-checked. On a static site with no plugin, the fix is procedural, not technical: the visible FAQ and its JSON-LD block change in the same edit, every time, no exceptions. I keep them in the same file, in the same commit, so there is no separate step to forget.

## How to validate without a plugin

No plugin means no dashboard warning you. So the validation step is manual and non-negotiable, and it takes about a minute per page:

One more practical note for static sites: JSON-LD is just JSON inside a script tag, so it breaks exactly like JSON breaks — a trailing comma, an unescaped quote in a description, a smart quote pasted from a word processor. If the testing tool reports nothing at all, the block probably failed to parse as JSON before it failed as schema. Check the JSON first.

## The whole recipe card

None of this needs a plugin, a build step, or a server. It needs three small blocks, kept honest, in the same files as the pages they describe. That is the whole trick — and on a static site, it is the only trick that stays true.

## Try it

I build NitroIDE — a browser-based IDE where your code never leaves your machine: nitroide.com

⭐ If you enjoyed this, star NitroIDE on GitHub: github.com/nitroideofficial/nitroide

## Frequently asked questions

### Do I need a plugin to add JSON-LD schema?

No. JSON-LD is just JSON inside a script tag on the page, so on a static site you write the block by hand in the same file as the page it describes — no plugin, build step, or server required.

### Which JSON-LD types does a static indie site need?

Three cover almost everything: SoftwareApplication for the product page, BlogPosting for every article, and FAQPage only where the page visibly answers questions.

### What voids a BlogPosting block?

Copy-paste without editing. It is the easiest block to clone across articles, which makes it the easiest to ship with the previous article's headline, description, or URL still in it. Check that mainEntityOfPage equals the URL of the page you are looking at.

### When should FAQPage schema be used?

Only where the page visibly contains those questions and answers, mirroring them exactly. If the visible FAQ changes and the schema does not, the page and its schema disagree in a format designed to be machine-checked.

### SEO Checklist for Indie Hackers: Sitemap, Schema, and llms.txt — the Three Files That Do the Talking
Source: https://nitroide.com/blog/seo-checklist-for-indie-hackers.html
Date: October 2026

Most indie SEO advice is a list of things to write: more posts, better titles, target this keyword. That advice is not wrong, exactly. It is just the second half of the job, and it assumes the first half already happened — that search engines and AI assistants can actually find, understand, and trust your pages.

I run NitroIDE, a browser IDE on a static host with no server, no build step, and no plugin system. There is no SEO plugin to install. Everything machine-readable on the site is a file I wrote by hand or a script I maintain. That constraint turned out to be useful: it forced me to learn which three files actually matter, what each one is for, and how each one silently breaks.

Here is the checklist, in the order I would do it again.

## 1. The sitemap: prove every page exists

A sitemap is a list of your URLs, with a last-modified date for each, handed to search engines in a format they can crawl without guessing. It does not make a bad page rank. It makes a good page findable — especially on a site where new pages arrive one at a time and internal linking is thin.

The checklist for a sitemap:

The mistake that silently voids a sitemap is staleness, not syntax. Syntax errors show up loudly in the report. A sitemap that is valid but three months old just quietly stops describing your site.

## 2. Schema: tell machines what the page IS

If the sitemap says “these pages exist,” schema says “and here is what each one is.” JSON-LD is the format: a block of structured data in the page that names the thing — a software product, a blog post, a FAQ — in a vocabulary search engines already understand.

For an indie site, three types cover almost everything:

Three rules for schema that I wish someone had given me earlier:

The mistake that silently voids schema is the same as the sitemap's, in a different costume: schema that describes last month's page. When you change a price, a version, or a headline, the schema changes in the same commit, or it becomes a lie told in a format machines trust.

## 3. llms.txt: the file for readers that are not browsers

Sitemaps and schema are for search engines. llms.txt is for a newer reader: AI assistants that want to understand your site without crawling every page and reconstructing the picture from fragments. It is a short, plain-text file at your site root that says what the site is, what its important pages are, and where to find them.

I added one recently, and it taught me something the other two files did not: a summary file is a second source of truth. A reader on Peerlist put it better than I did — llms.txt is like a contract summary versus the document itself. Useful, but only while it matches the document. The moment the site changes and the summary does not, the summary is not just stale, it is actively misleading the exact readers you wrote it for.

So the checklist for llms.txt is short and strict:

The mistake that silently voids llms.txt is neglect. Unlike a broken sitemap, which Search Console reports, a stale llms.txt produces no error. It just keeps answering questions about a site that no longer exists.

## The whole checklist, on one screen

None of this replaces writing something worth finding. But it is the difference between a good page that search engines and AI assistants can describe accurately, and a good page they have to guess at. Indie hackers do not have a marketing team to do the guessing for them. These three files are the team.

## Try it

I build NitroIDE — a browser-based IDE where your code never leaves your machine: nitroide.com

⭐ If you enjoyed this, star NitroIDE on GitHub: github.com/nitroideofficial/nitroide

## Frequently asked questions

### What three files does an indie site need for SEO?

A sitemap that proves every page exists, JSON-LD schema that says what each page is, and a short llms.txt that maps the site for AI readers. Together they cover findability, understanding, and trust.

### How should sitemap lastmod dates be set?

From a real source, such as git history: the last commit that touched each page sets its lastmod. A hand-edited date that never changes teaches crawlers to ignore your dates.

### When should FAQPage schema be used?

Only where the page genuinely answers questions visibly. Schema that describes content the page does not show is a mismatch waiting to be flagged.

### Why does a stale llms.txt matter?

Unlike a broken sitemap, a stale llms.txt produces no error. It just keeps answering questions about a site that no longer exists, misleading exactly the readers it was written for.

### Offline-First on GitHub Pages: What Actually Works (and Where It Honestly Ends)
Source: https://nitroide.com/blog/offline-first-github-pages.html
Date: October 2026

NitroIDE runs on GitHub Pages. That means there is no server: no Node process, no database, no code that runs on request. Pages are static files, and GitHub serves them exactly as they are — it cannot even set custom response headers, which is why my security headers live at the Cloudflare layer instead.

And yet the editor works offline. Open it once with a connection, kill your wifi, reload, and you can still write code, run the preview, and keep your projects. That is not magic and it is not a contradiction. It is a service worker doing a small number of jobs, each with a deliberate strategy — plus an honest list of things it cannot do.

Here is the recipe, including the parts where “offline-first” stops being true.

## What “offline” actually means here

First, the honest boundary: the first visit needs the network. A service worker cannot cache what the browser has never downloaded. Offline-first is a promise about the second visit onward, not the first. Anyone selling you “works offline” without that sentence is selling you the demo, not the product.

Once the shell is cached, the app itself — editor, preview, console, saved projects — needs no network at all. Projects live in localStorage (the subject of my Oct 22 article), the preview runs entirely client-side in a sandboxed iframe, and nothing phones home. The network is an input you may use, never a dependency the app waits on.

## Rule 1: precache the app shell, and only the app shell

On install, the service worker caches the small set of files the app cannot boot without: the HTML shell, the main script, the stylesheet. Everything else is cached on first use, not up front.

Precaching the world feels thorough and is actually harmful: a huge install step that can fail halfway, stale copies of files nobody opened, and a first visit that gets slower in the name of a later visit that may never come. Cache the boot path. Let the rest earn its place.

## Rule 2: network-first for your own code, cache-first for vendor code

This is the split that matters most, and it is the one I got wrong before I got it right.

Your own pages and your main script are network-first: try the network, fall back to the cache when it fails. The reason is the trap I wrote about on Oct 14 — a cache-first HTML file is how users get stuck on an old version of your app and never know it. Fresh code wins whenever the network exists; the cache is the fallback, not the authority.

Heavy vendor assets are the opposite: cache-first. Monaco, fonts, and icon files are large, change rarely, and are usually versioned by filename or path. Serving them from cache makes repeat loads fast, and a stale copy of a font is invisible in a way a stale copy of your app logic is not. Same cache, opposite strategies, decided file by file — not one global policy.

## Rule 3: version the cache and delete the old one

Every service worker version gets its own cache name, and on activation the worker deletes every cache that is not the current one. No migration, no merge, no “keep the last two just in case.”

This is what makes Rule 2 safe to live with: when you ship, the old world is removed in one step. Users are either on the new cache or they are about to be. The failure mode to fear is not “old cache lingers” — it is two versions of your app sharing state, which is exactly what the clean-slate activation prevents.

## Rule 4: never cache the API

NitroIDE's contact form posts to a Cloudflare Worker backend, and those /api/* requests bypass the cache entirely — never stored, never served stale.

This rule generalizes to anything with side effects or fresh state: form submissions, auth, anything that is not a static file. A cached POST response is a bug report waiting to happen, and a stale GET of “current state” is worse than a slow one. If it is not a file you shipped, do not put it in the file cache.

## Rule 5: cache navigations under the bare path

NitroIDE share links look like ?code=... — every shared snippet is a unique URL serving the same HTML shell. Cache each one separately and your cache grows with every link anyone opens, which is exactly the bloat the v25 audit fixed.

So document navigations are cached under the bare path, query string stripped. One entry serves every share link. The code itself rides in the URL, so nothing is lost — the shell is identical, and the snippet arrives with the navigation. Any app with share links, search params, or tracking params needs this rule or it will cache the same page a thousand times under a thousand names.

## Where it honestly ends

Offline-first on a static host has real edges, and you should say them out loud:

First load needs the network. No way around it. Your offline story starts at visit two.

Anything server-shaped needs the network. Form submissions, AI calls to a provider, importing a gist — all of these fail offline, and should fail loudly rather than silently pretending.

“Clear site data” wipes everything. The cache and localStorage go together. Offline persistence is not a backup; that is why NitroIDE exports to ZIP.

HTTPS and a registered scope are required. Service workers do not run on plain HTTP, and a worker only controls pages under its scope. Both are free on GitHub Pages — but they are requirements, not defaults you can skip.

Storage quotas exist. Browsers cap cache storage, and eviction under pressure is real. The shell is small by design; that is a feature, not an accident.

## How to test it (the part people skip)

Put the browser in offline mode in DevTools — not airplane mode on your whole machine, which also kills the DevTools connection in confusing ways — and do a normal reload, not a hard reload. A hard reload bypasses the service worker and tests nothing. Then check three things: the app boots, the editor works, and a previously opened project loads. Then go back online and confirm the new version arrives on the next visit — that is Rule 2 doing its job.

That test is the whole pitch in one gesture: no server, no signup, no connection — and the tool still works. The static host did not make that possible. A small, opinionated cache policy did.

## Try it

I build NitroIDE — a browser-based IDE where your code never leaves your machine: nitroide.com

⭐ If you enjoyed this, star NitroIDE on GitHub: github.com/nitroideofficial/nitroide

## Frequently asked questions

### Can a static site on GitHub Pages really work offline?

Yes, after the first visit: a service worker caches the app shell and serves it when the network is gone. The first visit always needs the network — a worker cannot cache what the browser has never downloaded.

### Should HTML pages be cache-first or network-first?

Network-first for your own pages and scripts, so users never get silently trapped on an old version. Cache-first suits heavy vendor assets like Monaco, fonts, and icons, which change rarely and are harmless if briefly stale.

### What should a service worker never cache?

Anything with side effects or fresh state — API calls, form submissions, auth. A cached POST response is a bug waiting to happen, and a stale GET of current state is worse than a slow one.

### How do you test offline mode properly?

Use DevTools offline mode and do a normal reload, not a hard reload — a hard reload bypasses the service worker and tests nothing. Then check the app boots, the editor works, and a previously opened project loads.

### localStorage Is My Database (For Now)
Source: https://nitroide.com/blog/localstorage-as-database.html
Date: October 2026

NitroIDE has no server and no database. Your projects still survive a browser restart, a closed tab, and a Monday morning. The entire persistence layer is localStorage — one API, string keys, string values, about 5 MB per origin.

That sounds like a toy. It has carried a real product for months. It has also taught me exactly where it breaks, because I have hit every wall myself. Here is the honest version: the patterns that work, the limits that bite, and the line where you graduate to something bigger.

## Pattern 1: one key, one JSON document

The first mistake is treating localStorage like a table and scattering dozens of keys. I do the opposite: one key holds one whole document.

NitroIDE's projects live under a single key, nitro_projects — a JSON array where each project carries its virtual file system (its HTML, CSS, and JS files). A second key, nitro_current_project_id, tracks which project is active. Loading the app is two reads and two parses. Saving is one JSON.stringify and one write.

The tradeoff is real and you should name it: every save rewrites the whole document. For a handful of projects with small files, that is milliseconds and nobody notices. For a megabyte of code, it is a full re-serialize on every save — which is why Pattern 4 exists.

## Pattern 2: namespace every key, and never trust what's inside

Preferences live under their own namespaced keys — theme, nitro_font, nitroide_wordwrap — so a key never collides with another feature's data or with a library's. The nitro_ prefix is the whole scheme, and it is enough.

More important: every read is wrapped in try/catch with a sane default. localStorage is user-editable, extensions can touch it, and a half-written value from a crashed tab is a JSON.parse error waiting to happen. Corrupt data must degrade to “fresh default project”, never to a white screen. If your app cannot boot with an empty store, your store is a single point of failure.

## Pattern 3: cap your history before it caps you

Unbounded growth is how a 5 MB store dies. NitroIDE's time-machine snapshots are sliced to a fixed length before every save — old history is dropped as new history arrives, by construction, not by a cleanup job I might forget to run.

The rule generalizes: any list you append to in localStorage needs a cap at write time. Undo stacks, recent files, activity logs — if it grows without a ceiling, it will eventually throw QuotaExceededError at the worst possible moment, which is always mid-save.

## Pattern 4: don't save on every keystroke

Saves are batched, not fired per keystroke. Typing is fast; serializing a whole project document is not free, and localStorage is synchronous — every write blocks the main thread until it finishes. A big document saved on every keypress is a typing lag bug wearing a persistence costume.

Batching plus the whole-document rewrite is the core tension of this design: simple reads, expensive writes. Keep documents small, save on pauses, and measure before you blame the editor.

## The limits, stated plainly

About 5 MB per origin. Browsers vary, and the count is roughly in UTF-16 code units, so non-ASCII text costs more than you think. There is no “buy more” button.

Strings only. Everything is serialized. Dates become strings, undefined vanishes from JSON, and a Map silently becomes {}. If your data model needs types, your serialization layer is now part of your database.

Synchronous and blocking. There is no async localStorage. A large read on startup delays first paint; a large write freezes typing. This is the limit that ends the honeymoon.

No queries, no indexes, no transactions. Finding one project means parsing all of them. Two tabs writing at once can clobber each other — the storage event tells other tabs something changed, but it does not merge anything.

Per-origin, and wiped with site data. http and https are different stores, subdomains are different stores, and “clear site data” deletes everything. It is a cache with delusions of permanence unless you also offer export — which is why NitroIDE exports to ZIP.

Readable by any script on your origin. This is the security line. localStorage has no per-key permissions: any XSS on your page reads the whole store. Never put tokens or secrets in it. And this is exactly why NitroIDE's preview iframe runs on an opaque origin — user code in the preview cannot reach the parent's localStorage at all. The sandbox fix from the v25 audit and the storage design are the same decision: the store is only as safe as the origin around it.

## When to graduate

Move on when any one of these turns true: you need queries or indexes, you store more than a few megabytes, you store binary data, or two tabs must transact without clobbering each other. IndexedDB is the usual next step — async, much larger, indexed, transactional — and it is a real database with real API surface to show for it.

My rule of thumb: localStorage is a database for documents you can hold in your head — settings, small project lists, drafts. The moment you catch yourself building an index, a migration, or a merge strategy on top of it, you have already outgrown it. Build the index in a store that has one.

Until that day, though, one key per document, namespaced keys, try/catch on every read, a cap on every list, and batched saves will carry you further than most people expect. It carried a whole IDE.

## Try it

I build NitroIDE — a browser-based IDE where your code never leaves your machine: nitroide.com

⭐ If you enjoyed this, star NitroIDE on GitHub: github.com/nitroideofficial/nitroide

## Frequently asked questions

### How much can localStorage actually hold?

About 5 MB per origin, counted roughly in UTF-16 code units, so non-ASCII text costs more than you think. There is no way to buy more — when the store is full, writes throw QuotaExceededError.

### Why does NitroIDE save whole documents instead of individual files?

One key per JSON document keeps reads to two parses and writes to one stringify. The cost is that every save rewrites the whole document, which is why saves are batched instead of fired per keystroke.

### What should never go in localStorage?

Tokens and secrets: any script on your origin can read the whole store, so an XSS anywhere reads everything. NitroIDE's preview iframe runs on an opaque origin precisely so user code cannot reach the parent's store.

### When should I switch from localStorage to IndexedDB?

When you need queries or indexes, more than a few megabytes, binary data, or safe multi-tab writes. If you catch yourself building an index, a migration, or a merge strategy on top of localStorage, you have already outgrown it.

### I Built a Blog Engine With No Build Step
Source: https://nitroide.com/blog/vanilla-js-blog-engine.html
Date: October 2026

There's no CMS behind this blog. No static site generator, no build step, no database. Thirty-seven posts, and the entire "engine" is five files plus a checklist.

That's not a brag — it's a design I can explain in one sitting, and if you run a docs site or a personal blog on a static host, you can steal the whole pattern today.

## The five files

One JSON file is the brain. blog/blog-data.json holds one object per post — slug, meta title and description, keywords, category, date, an HTML excerpt, a per-post theme color, and per-post CTA fields. Thirty-seven entries. Every list on the site renders from this file.

Each post is its own HTML page. blog/<slug>.html — fully self-contained, with its own meta tags and OG tags. No templates rendered server-side, no build injecting headers. Open view-source on any post and you're looking at the whole thing.

The index renders client-side. blog/index.html fetches blog-data.json, dedupes entries by slug (a line that exists because duplicates have genuinely happened), and renders the card grid. One fetch, one file, no framework.

RSS is a hand-edited file with a gate in front of it. rss.xml carries all 37 items, maintained by hand. The comment at the top of the file says it plainly: before committing, run python3 -c "import xml.dom.minidom; xml.dom.minidom.parse('rss.xml')" — it must exit 0. Then a second check counts <item> opens against closes, because the gate comment itself mentions <item> and would corrupt a naive count. This gate exists because the live feed broke three times — Sep 2026, Oct 8, Oct 10 — a missing closing tag every time. Automation doesn't have to be clever. It has to remember the last three times you broke it.

The sitemap gets honest dates from git. Eighty-six URLs in sitemap.xml, each <lastmod> derived from git log -1 --format=%cs -- <file>. I wrote the full recipe for that one separately — the short version is: a sitemap that claims everything changed today teaches crawlers to stop trusting it.

## The decision I'm proudest of: the noscript list

JavaScript renders the card grid — so what does a visitor without JS see? A blank page would be the failure mode. Googlebot runs JavaScript these days, but simpler crawlers and real no-JS users don't.

So blog/index.html carries a <noscript> block: every article as a plain link, newest first, with a comment in the source that says "Regenerate from blog-data.json when publishing (keep in sync with the JS grid above)". JS visitors see the card grid instead — the page deliberately never shows both. One list for humans with JS, one plain list for everyone else, no duplicate listing.

There's also a hardcoded three-card "Latest articles" row for featured posts — not from the JSON, chosen by hand. Some curation refuses to be automated.

## The honest part: the maintenance tax

Here's what five files cost you. Every new post touches five places: the HTML file, the JSON entry, the RSS item (gated), the sitemap URL, and the noscript list. All hand-synced. There is no build to catch the drift — the publishing checklist is the build.

That sounds worse than it is. A checklist you run in two minutes, in exchange for: zero dependencies, zero build minutes, zero framework upgrades, and every failure mode debuggable with view-source. The engine has no moving parts, so nothing can break while you're asleep. The worst failure is a post missing from one list — visible, obvious, fixed in one commit.

## The stealable pattern

If you're building a docs site or a blog on a static host: one JSON index, client-side render, a <noscript> mirror list for crawlers and no-JS users, an RSS file with a parse gate (not vibes), and sitemap dates from git history. No build step required. The checklist is the build.

## Try it

I build NitroIDE — a browser-based IDE where your code never leaves your machine: nitroide.com

⭐ If you enjoyed this, star NitroIDE on GitHub: github.com/nitroideofficial/nitroide

## Frequently asked questions

### How do you run a blog with no CMS and no build step?

With five files: one JSON file (blog-data.json) as the index, one self-contained HTML page per post, a client-side-rendered index page, a hand-edited RSS file, and a sitemap. The publishing checklist replaces the build step — every post is verified against each file before it ships.

### How do search engines read a blog index that renders with JavaScript?

They don't have to: blog/index.html carries a <noscript> block with every article as a plain link, regenerated from blog-data.json at publish time. JS visitors see the card grid instead — the page never shows both.

### How do you keep a hand-edited RSS feed from breaking?

With a validation gate before every commit: the file must parse as XML, and the count of <item> opens must equal closes. The gate exists because the live feed broke three times — Sep 2026, Oct 8, and Oct 10 — a missing closing tag each time.

### Where do the sitemap's lastmod dates come from?

From git history: each URL's <lastmod> is derived from git log -1 --format=%cs for that file. A sitemap that claims everything changed today teaches crawlers to stop trusting it.

### 12 Starters, Zero Blank Pages: A Tour of NitroIDE's Template Gallery
Source: https://nitroide.com/blog/templates-gallery-tour.html
Date: October 2026

The hardest part of any project is the blank page. Not the hard algorithm, not the deployment — the empty editor, blinking at you, daring you to type something.

NitroIDE's template gallery exists to kill that moment. Twelve starters, each one opening directly in the browser IDE with working code and a live preview. No signup, no download, no "create project" wizard. Pick one, and you're editing within seconds.

This is a tour of all twelve — not what they are, but when to reach for each. Because a template you pick for the wrong reason is just a fancier blank page.

## How templates work

Every template in the gallery is a link of the form codebox.html?template=<slug>. Open it, and the IDE loads with that template's code already in the editor and the preview already running. Edit anything and the preview updates instantly. When you're done, export to ZIP or share a live ?code= link — the same flow as any project you build from scratch.

There are no accounts, no saved-to-cloud state, nothing to configure. Templates are starting points, not finished products: the expectation is that you change them, break them, and delete the parts you don't need. That's the point.

## Websites: when you need something presentable today

Personal Portfolio — a clean single-page portfolio with hero, work grid, about, and contact sections. Reach for this when you need a presentable personal site by tonight. It is the best first template if you've never shipped a site: the structure is the standard one, and swapping in your own work is the whole job.

Startup Landing Page — a modern SaaS landing page with hero, feature cards, stats, and a signup form. Reach for this when you need to pitch something — a product, a project, an idea you want signups for. Every SaaS landing follows this shape; starting from it means you argue about your copy, not your layout.

Link in Bio — a polished personal links page: avatar, name, bio, link buttons, social icons. Dark, mobile-first. Reach for this when one link has to do the work of five — the link in your social bio, on your resume, in your email signature. It is the smallest template with the highest immediate usefulness.

## Apps and tools: when you're learning by building something real

Todo App — a vanilla JS todo list with add, complete, delete, and localStorage persistence. Reach for this when you're learning state: it's the smallest app that teaches real patterns — a list in memory, rendering from state, persistence across reloads. Every framework tutorial uses a todo for a reason; this one has no framework in the way.

Analog + Digital Clock — a smooth animated analog clock face with a live digital readout. Reach for this when you want to see animation done with code — timers, transforms, and a face that redraws every second. A good template for learning how setInterval and CSS transforms cooperate.

CSS Gradient Generator — an interactive tool: pick colors and angle, preview the gradient, copy the CSS. Reach for this when you need a tool, not a demo. This is the template I point at when someone asks whether templates are "real" — it is genuinely useful as-is, and its code is a clean lesson in wiring inputs to a live preview.

Markdown Previewer — type Markdown on the left, watch it render as HTML on the right, live. Reach for this when you want to learn two-way live rendering: input in, transformed output out, no save button anywhere. The pattern shows up everywhere — editors, playgrounds, form builders.

Countdown Timer — an event countdown with big glowing digits. Set any target date and time, persisted in localStorage. Reach for this when you need a deadline widget — a launch, an exam, a birthday. The persistence is the lesson: close the tab, come back, the countdown is still yours.

## Experiments: when you want to try something without the toolchain

Pure CSS Sunset — a mountain sunset scene drawn entirely with CSS gradients and clip-path, with a day/night toggle. Reach for this when you want to learn what CSS alone can draw. No images, no canvas — just gradients and shapes. It is the template that most surprises people, and the best argument that "CSS art" is a real skill.

Target Tap Game — a tiny canvas game: click the targets before the 30-second timer runs out. Reach for this when you want to learn game loops — canvas drawing, timers, click handling, score state. It is small enough to read in one sitting and complete enough to feel like a game.

Tailwind via CDN — Tailwind CSS loaded from CDN: utility-first cards, buttons, and a counter. Reach for this when you want to try Tailwind without a build step. No npm, no config, no purge setup — just utility classes in a working page, so you can decide whether you like the style before committing to the toolchain.

React 18 Counter — React 18 loaded from CDN with hooks: a working counter, no build step or JSX compiler. Reach for this when you want React without the toolchain. Same logic as the Tailwind template — try the real thing, in the browser, before you install anything. If hooks click for you here, then go set up a real project.

## The one rule for picking

Match the template to what you're actually building or learning — not the shiniest one. A portfolio template won't teach you state; a todo app won't land you a client. And once you've picked: delete what you don't need. A template is a head start, not a contract. The fastest way to make any of these yours is to remove the parts that aren't your project.

## What templates are not

They're not finished products, and they're not a design system. They're twelve starting points with honest, readable code — no hidden magic, no lock-in. And the gallery is open to submissions: if you've built something in NitroIDE that would make a good starting point for someone else, there's a "Submit your template" card at the bottom of the gallery.

Twelve starters. Zero blank pages. Pick one and start editing.

### Zero Security Headers to a Hardened Static Site: The Cloudflare Recipe I Run on NitroIDE
Source: https://nitroide.com/blog/cloudflare-security-headers-recipe.html
Date: October 2026

GitHub Pages is a wonderful host with one sharp edge: it cannot set HTTP response headers. Not one. Your site ships with zero security headers unless you add a layer in front of it that can.

I build NitroIDE — a browser-based IDE where your code never leaves your machine. When I audited my own site for the v25 release, the header situation was blunt: none. No HSTS, no nosniff, no referrer policy, nothing. This post is the full recipe I run today, header by header, with the exact values, what each one stops, the price I paid for the strict ones, and the two headers I deliberately left out.

## Where the headers live

Cloudflare sits in front of nitroide.com, and Cloudflare's Transform Rules → Modify Response Header is where every header below is set. One rule, applied to all responses, no code changes, no redeploy to change a value.

Two alternatives I ruled out: a _headers file only works if your host reads it (Cloudflare Pages does; GitHub Pages does not — my origin ignores it), and <meta http-equiv> tags in HTML only cover a couple of headers and don't apply to non-HTML responses. If your static site is behind Cloudflare, the Transform Rule is the one place that covers everything.

## The recipe

HSTS — Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains

Forces the browser to use HTTPS for the next year, for this domain and every subdomain. It kills SSL-stripping and downgrade attacks — the kind where an attacker on public Wi-Fi serves your site over plain HTTP and the user never notices. One deliberate omission: no preload. Preload is a one-way door — once you're on the browser preload list, every subdomain must serve valid HTTPS forever, and removal takes months. One year + includeSubDomains is the strong posture without the irreversible commitment.

MIME sniffing — X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff

Stops browsers from second-guessing your Content-Type. Without it, a browser can decide a file you served as text/plain is actually a script and execute it — the classic vector for turning an upload or a user-content endpoint into code execution. One word, no downside. There is no reason to skip this one.

Referrer — Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin

Same-origin requests send the full URL; cross-origin requests send only the origin. Your analytics and your own logs keep the detail, but when a user clicks out to another site, that site learns they came from nitroide.com — not which page, not which ?code= share link, not which query string. Share links carry user code; leaking their full path in a referrer would be a quiet privacy hole.

Permissions — Permissions-Policy: camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=()

Turns off powerful browser features the site never uses. NitroIDE is a code editor — it has no reason to request your camera, microphone, or location, so the browser is told upfront that those requests are denied. This is least-privilege at the platform layer: even if a third-party script or a future feature tried, the browser says no.

Cross-origin isolation — Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin + Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp

This is the strict pair, and the one that costs something. Together they give the page cross-origin isolation: other origins can't hold a live reference to your window, and your page refuses to load any cross-origin subresource unless that resource explicitly opts in (via a Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy header or CORS). What it buys is protection against a whole class of cross-origin read attacks — the Spectre family — and a stronger guarantee that the code running in your tab is only the code you shipped.

The price is real, and I paid it. COEP require-corp breaks anything cross-origin that doesn't opt in: a font, a CDN script, an analytics pixel, an embed. I have personally debugged a COEP/CORP failure on this site where a legitimate resource silently failed to load and the page just looked broken, with no error pointing at the header. The fix is discipline, not a weaker header: serve everything you can same-origin, and for anything genuinely cross-origin, make sure it sends Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy or is fetched in CORS mode. If you set COEP and something breaks, check the resource's headers before you blame your code — that is the single most useful debugging rule in this whole post.

Cloudflare also appends Report-To / NEL (Network Error Logging) headers automatically. They're telemetry about failed requests, not a header I configured — I leave them alone.

## What I deliberately left out

No Content-Security-Policy — yet. This is the honest part. CSP is the most powerful header on this list and the easiest to get wrong. A bad CSP breaks your product: blocked scripts, dead embeds, templates that silently stop working. A missing CSP breaks nothing. NitroIDE loads user code, templates, CDN libraries, and embeds — I want to test a CSP against every one of those before enforcing it. It is on the list; it is not shipped on a hope.

No X-Frame-Options. It is legacy. The modern replacement is CSP's frame-ancestors, which lands with the CSP work above. Shipping the old header now would be theater — one more line that looks like security without the policy behind it.

## Verify it yourself

Headers are claims. Verify them the way I did, in one command:

curl -sI https://nitroide.com/
 You should see all six headers in the response. For a second opinion, run the URL through a header scanner (OWASP's Secure Headers Project and securityheaders.com both grade the same set) — but read the findings, don't chase the letter grade. A scanner will flag the missing CSP; you now know why it's missing, and "missing on purpose, tracked" beats "added to silence the scanner, breaking the product."

## The copy-paste version

Six headers, one Transform Rule, zero code changes. The first four are free — no downside, no debugging, no reason not to ship them today. The last two are the ones that earn their keep: set them, then budget an hour for the cross-origin resource that will surprise you.

Further reading: MDN's guides on HSTS, Permissions-Policy, and cross-origin isolation with COOP/COEP, plus the OWASP Secure Headers Project.

CSP is the most powerful header and the easiest to get wrong. A bad CSP breaks the product: blocked scripts, dead embeds, templates that silently stop working. A missing CSP breaks nothing. NitroIDE loads user code, templates, CDN libraries, and embeds — the policy will ship once it is tested against all of them, not to silence a scanner.

### Why no X-Frame-Options header?

X-Frame-Options is legacy. The modern replacement is CSP's frame-ancestors directive, which lands with the CSP work. Shipping the old header now would be theater — one more line that looks like security without the policy behind it.

### What does COEP require-corp break?

Any cross-origin subresource that doesn't opt in: a font, a CDN script, an analytics pixel, an embed. Preload is a one-way door — once you're on the browser preload list, every subdomain must serve valid HTTPS forever, and removal takes months. One year + includeSubDomains is the strong posture without the irreversible commitment.

### HMR Without a Bundler: How NitroIDE's Instant Preview Updates Actually Work
Source: https://nitroide.com/blog/hmr-without-a-bundler.html
Date: October 2026

Type a character in Vite and the browser updates before your finger leaves the key. It feels like magic, but it isn't — it's a dev server, a WebSocket, a module graph, and a client runtime, all cooperating to patch the running page instead of reloading it.

NitroIDE does the same trick with none of that. No dev server. No WebSocket. No module graph. No bundler at all. The whole update loop is a debounced timer, a string concatenation, and an iframe attribute. Here's the entire thing — including the one place it cheats, honestly labeled.

## The pipeline is five steps

I build NitroIDE, a browser-based IDE where your code never leaves your machine. The editor is Monaco, the preview is a sandboxed iframe, and every file lives in an in-memory virtual filesystem. The update loop starts the moment you type:

No server round-trip, because there is no server. No file watcher, because the files were never on disk. The "bundler" is three loops and a template literal.

## CSS gets true HMR. HTML and JS get a fast full reload.

Here's the honest split, because the word HMR gets abused.

When you edit CSS, the preview does not rebuild at all. queueUpdate takes a shortcut: it posts { type: "update-css", css: collectCSS() } to the live iframe, and the injected bridge script inside the preview replaces the <style id="live-css-inject"> tag's text with the fresh CSS. The page never reloads. Your JavaScript keeps running — timers keep ticking, form inputs keep their values, scroll position stays put, and the console panel isn't even cleared. That is real hot module replacement, implemented in about three lines.

When you edit HTML or JS, the preview rebuilds from scratch via srcdoc. Everything re-runs: the DOM is rebuilt, your script executes from the top, timers restart, form state resets, and the console clears first so stale logs can't masquerade as fresh ones. It's a full reload — just one that costs a string concatenation and a srcdoc assignment instead of a network round-trip, so it still lands in about 200ms.

I don't pretend the JS path is HMR. It isn't. But the split is the right one: CSS is the thing you tweak fifty times while staring at pixels, so CSS is the thing that gets the state-preserving path. HTML and JS edits are rarer and semantically bigger, so they get the clean-slate path.

## The swap is flicker-free by construction

The naive version of the srcdoc rebuild has an obvious flaw: assigning srcdoc blanks the iframe while the new document parses, so every keystroke would flash the preview white. The fix is a double-buffered swap:

No white flash, no half-painted frames, no out-of-order previews. The user sees the preview change, never the machinery changing it.

## What the sandbox allows — and what it costs

The preview iframe runs with sandbox="allow-scripts allow-modals allow-popups allow-forms" — notably, no allow-same-origin. I removed that during the v25 security audit, because same-origin preview code could read the parent's localStorage. The preview still runs your JavaScript and renders your page, but on an opaque origin, talking to the parent only through postMessage (console logs, errors, state-watcher updates, the CSS hot-patch).

That isolation is also why the CSS hot-patch works so cleanly: the parent can't reach into the iframe's DOM, so the update has to be a message, and a message carrying "here is the new stylesheet" is exactly the right granularity.

## The honest ceiling

Every tool should state its ceiling, so here it is:

## Why this shape, and not a real HMR runtime?

Because the constraints chose it. A browser IDE with no server can't run a dev server; an IDE that opens in one click can't ask you to install a watcher; an IDE whose files live in memory doesn't need one. The moment I accepted "the build step is string concatenation, the deploy step is srcdoc", every piece fell into place: debounce instead of a watcher, postMessage instead of a socket, a hidden-iframe swap instead of a virtual DOM diff.

The lesson I keep relearning: the fastest feedback loop isn't the one with the most sophisticated machinery. It's the one with the fewest moving parts between your keystroke and the pixels. Ours has five steps, zero servers, and a 200ms timer — and it has never once needed a config file.

## Try it

NitroIDE is free, no signup, and your code runs only in your browser: nitroide.com

⭐ If you enjoyed this, star NitroIDE on GitHub: github.com/nitroideofficial/nitroide

## Frequently asked questions

### Does NitroIDE have real HMR?

For CSS, yes — the parent postMessages the fresh stylesheet and the preview swaps one style tag's text with no reload and no state loss. HTML and JS edits get a fast full reload instead, which is deliberately not called HMR.

### Why do HTML and JS edits reset the preview's state?

Because those edits rebuild the preview from scratch via srcdoc: the DOM is rebuilt, scripts re-run from the top, timers restart, and form state resets. That clean slate is the point — you always see a fresh run.

### Does NitroIDE use a dev server or bundler?

No. The build step is string concatenation of the in-memory files and the deploy step is assigning the result to the preview iframe's srcdoc attribute. There is no server, no watcher, and no config file.

### Why doesn't the preview flash white on every keystroke?

Rebuilds render into a hidden iframe first; after its load event plus two requestAnimationFrame ticks, the new iframe is promoted and the old one removed. A generation counter discards stale rebuilds overtaken by newer typing.
